changeSet.author: VanillaBP
changeSet.comment: The phase-two outbox of a remote BPMS: one entry per operation which may only reach the BPMS after the caller's transaction committed. DEDUP_KEY is what makes a duplicate schedule a no-op: it holds the entry's idempotency key while the entry waits for its dispatch and the entry's own ID once it was dispatched, so the unique constraint spans exactly the operations which are still planned - a repetition after the dispatch is a new operation (see decision 22 of the repository). It is never null, which is what keeps a database treating two nulls as equal out of the picture. IDEMPOTENCY_KEY carries the derived key for whoever reads the table during support and stays readable after the dispatch; its 512 characters stay below MySQL's index key-length limit.

changeSet.author: VanillaBP
changeSet.comment: The log of processed task deliveries: what a BPMS repeating a delivery is answered from. The delivery key is the BPMS' identity of the delivery, 512 characters for the same index reason. RECORDED_AT is the moment the handler ran and never moves, because the age of a task left open is measured from it; LAST_SEEN_AT is the moment the BPMS last redelivered that task, and the retention deletes by it, so a task which is still being redelivered keeps its record.

changeSet.author: VanillaBP
changeSet.comment: What the record says about the task it was written for. TASK_ID is the BPMS' identity of that task - what the application receives in a @TaskId parameter and passes back to complete or cancel it - and it is what lets VanillaBP answer from the record which BPMS holds a task, instead of asking every configured one per operation. TASK_CLOSED_AT is written once the application's completion or cancellation reached the BPMS, so a repeated completion is the warned no-op it always was without asking anybody either. Both are nullable: a record written before them knows neither, and is simply not part of an answer. A changeset of its own rather than columns added to the one above, because that one was applied already.

changeSet.author: VanillaBP
changeSet.comment: What the dispatcher of this table asks on every wake-up. Two indexes and not one, because the two questions filter the same STATUS and order by different columns: an entry waiting for its dispatch is found by NEXT_ATTEMPT_AT, an entry waiting to be deleted by DONE_AT, and one index over both timestamps would serve neither. Measured on PostgreSQL 16 with 200000 rows, the aggregate asking when the next entry is due took 11 to 18 ms as a sequential scan and 0.05 ms with the first of these - and the scan grows with the table while the index does not, which is what decision 19 of the repository forbids a repeated question to do. The same columns serve the selects which pick the due entries up and the delete which ends the retention. A changeset of its own rather than indexes added to the one above, because that one was applied already.

changeSet.author: VanillaBP
changeSet.comment: The index the retention of this table deletes by, which the runtime creates with the table and this changelog did not. An application applying the changelog therefore had the table the runtime builds minus one index, and the hourly delete was a scan growing with everything ever recorded. What the period has to cover is the same either way (see decision 24 of the repository); what differs is what the delete costs.
